# Constant variables

## Some values should never change

So far, every variable could be changed at any time:

```{.cpp}
double x{42.0};
x = 24.0;        // fine: x is meant to change

double gravity{9.81};
gravity = 1.89;  // allowed... but gravity shouldn't change!

double pi{3.1415926535};
pi = 3.0;        // some engineers do see pi as 3.0, but we don't want that!
```

A **constant** is a value that can't change while the program runs. C++ has two kinds:

- **named constants**, which have a name (this section);
- **literal constants**, or just **literals**, written straight into the code, like `9.81` (next section).

## Declaring a constant variable

Put the keyword `const` (the **const qualifier**) next to the type:

```{.cpp}
const double gravity{9.81};    // the usual style
int const sides_in_square{4};  // also legal, but less common
```

- `const` can go before or after the type. Before is more common: think "a green ball", not "a ball green".
- `const` is part of the type: the type of `gravity` is `const double`.

## A `const` variable must be initialized

You can't assign to a `const` variable, so it must get its value when it's defined:

```{.cpp filename="const_must_be_initialized.cpp" .no-compile}
{{< include ./cpp/const_must_be_initialized.cpp >}}
```

```{.text .output .compiler}
error: uninitialized 'const gravity' [-fpermissive]
error: assignment of read-only variable 'gravity'
```

## Initializing from a variable

A `const` variable can be initialized with any value, even one that's only known when the program runs:

```{.cpp filename="initialize_const_variables.cpp" .no-compile}
{{< include ./cpp/initialize_const_variables.cpp >}}
```

```{.text .output .compiler}
error: assignment of read-only variable 'const_age'
```

## Naming constants

You'll meet several conventions:

- `EARTH_GRAVITY`: upper case with underscores, popular with programmers coming from C;
- `kEarthGravity`: a "k" prefix, common in some C++ style guides;
- `earth_gravity`: just like any other variable.

My take: a `const` variable behaves like a normal variable except that it can't be assigned to, so it doesn't need a special name. Your IDE will tell you it's `const` anyway. In this course we use `snake_case` for constants too.

## `const` value parameters

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
```{.cpp filename="const_func_parameters.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/const_func_parameters.cpp >}}
```
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
```{.text .output}
42
```
:::
:::

- A `const` **value parameter** can't be changed inside the function.
- But it's only a copy (pass by value, Chapter 02): whatever the function does to it, nobody outside can tell. So the `const` adds clutter and protects nothing.

## `const` return values

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
```{.cpp filename="const_return_value.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/const_return_value.cpp >}}
```
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
```{.text .output .compiler}
warning: type qualifiers
ignored on function
return type
```
:::
:::

A `const` return value of a fundamental type is simply ignored, and `-Wextra` says so.

::: {.callout-tip title="Best practice"}
Don't use `const` on value parameters or on values returned by value. (`const` *references* are a different story: Chapter 07.)
:::

## Why make variables constant?

> **If a variable can be made constant, it generally should be.**

::: {.incremental}
- **No accidents.** Nobody, including you, can change it by mistake.
- **Faster programs.** When the compiler knows a value won't change, it can optimize more.
- **Simpler code.** When you're reading or debugging, a `const` variable is one less moving part: you never have to ask whether, where or to what it changed.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Look at well-written open-source C++ libraries on GitHub: you'll see `const` almost everywhere.
:::

## `constexpr`: constants known at compile time

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
```{.cpp filename="constexpr_example.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/constexpr_example.cpp >}}
```
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
```{.text .terminal}
$ ./constexpr_example
Radius: 2
Area: 12.5664
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Best practice"}
`constexpr` for values known at compile time, `const` for the rest.
:::
:::
:::

- A `constexpr` variable needs a value the compiler can work out **while compiling**, like `9.81` or `std::numbers::pi` (from `<numbers>`, C++20: don't type `pi` yourself!).
- `area` depends on user input, so it's only known when the program **runs**: it can be `const` but not `constexpr`.

# Literals

## Literals

A **literal** is a value written directly in the code. Like a variable, every literal has a type, and C++ works it out from how the literal is written:

| Literal | Type | Literal | Type |
|---------|------|---------|------|
| `42` | `int` | `'A'` | `char` (single quotes) |
| `42u` | `unsigned int` | `"Hello"` | text (double quotes) |
| `3.14` | `double` | `true`, `false` | `bool` |
| `3.14f` | `float` | `1.5e3` | `double` (1500.0) |

::: {.callout-note title="Coming from Python"}
In Python, `'A'` and `"A"` mean the same thing. In C++ they don't: single quotes make one `char`, double quotes make text.
:::

## Magic numbers

Remember `if (height >= 140)` from Chapter 03? What is `140`: a height, a weight, an age? A literal with no explanation is a **magic number**, and if the rule changes, you have to hunt down every copy.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
```{.cpp filename="magic_numbers.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/magic_numbers.cpp >}}
```
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
```{.text .terminal}
$ ./magic_numbers
Enter your height (in cm): 120
Sorry, too short to ride.
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Best practice"}
Give magic numbers a name with `constexpr`.
:::
:::
:::

# Strings

## `std::string`: text in C++

![](figures/string_chars.png){fig-alt="The string Khiem drawn as five boxes, K, h, i, e and m, labelled name[0] to name[4]. name.length() is 5 and the first index is 0." width="82%"}

- A `std::string` holds a piece of text: a sequence of characters, numbered from **0**.
- It lives in the standard library, so `#include <string>`.

## Your first strings

```{.cpp filename="string_basics.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/string_basics.cpp >}}
```

```{.text .output}
Hello, Khiem
Hello, Ada Lovelace
Ada Lovelace has 12 characters
```

- A string can change, and it grows or shrinks as needed: no need to say how long it is.
- `name.length()` tells you how many characters it holds. (It counts the space too.)

## Joining, indexing and comparing

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="72%"}
```{.cpp filename="string_operations.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/string_operations.cpp >}}
```
:::
::: {.column width="28%"}
```{.text .output}
Khiem Nguyen
First letter: K
Hello, lecturer!
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Coming from Python"}
`+` joins and `==` compares, as in Python; `len(s)` becomes `s.length()`. But a C++ string can be changed in place (Python strings can't), and `s[-1]` does **not** give the last character: there are no negative indices.
:::

## Reading a string: `>>` stops at a space

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
```{.cpp filename="string_input_cin.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/string_input_cin.cpp >}}
```
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
```{.text .terminal}
$ ./string_input_cin
Enter your full name: Khiem Nguyen
Hello, Khiem
```
:::
:::

Where did "Nguyen" go? `>>` reads one *word*: it stops at the first space, and the rest stays in the input buffer (remember Chapter 01?).

## `std::getline` reads the whole line

![](figures/cin_vs_getline.png){fig-alt="The typed input Khiem, space, Nguyen, Enter. std::cin >> name takes only Khiem and leaves the rest in the buffer. std::getline takes Khiem space Nguyen, up to the Enter, which it throws away." width="85%"}

To read text that may contain spaces, use `std::getline(std::cin, name)`. It reads everything up to the Enter key.

## Watch out: mixing `>>` and `std::getline`

```{.cpp filename="string_input_getline_bug.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/string_input_getline_bug.cpp >}}
```

```{.text .terminal}
$ ./string_input_getline_bug
Enter your age: 35
Enter your full name: Hello, , age 35
```

The program didn't even wait for the name! `>>` read `35` but left the **Enter** in the buffer, and `std::getline` happily read that empty line.

## The fix: `std::ws`

```{.cpp filename="string_input_getline.cpp"}
{{< include ./cpp/string_input_getline.cpp >}}
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{.text .terminal}
$ ./string_input_getline
Enter your age: 35
Enter your full name: Khiem Nguyen
Hello, Khiem Nguyen, age 35
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Best practice"}
`std::ws` skips leftover spaces and Enters, so this works whatever came before.
:::
:::
:::

## Strings and functions

```{.cpp}
void print_greeting(std::string name) { // pass by value: a copy
    std::cout << "Hello, " << name << '\n';
}
```

- Passing a `std::string` by value works, but it **copies** every character. For a name that's nothing; for a whole book it's slow.
- In Chapter 07 we'll learn to pass strings without copying them, using **references**. C++17 also offers `std::string_view`, a cheap read-only view of a string.
- Until then, passing strings by value is fine.

# Wrapping up

## Summary

- `const` makes a variable read-only. It must be initialized, and **if a variable can be `const`, it should be**.
- `constexpr` is for values known at compile time; `const` for the rest. Get `pi` from `<numbers>`.
- Don't put `const` on value parameters or on return values.
- Every literal has a type: `'A'` is a `char`, `"A"` is text. Replace magic numbers with named `constexpr` constants.
- `std::string` holds text: `+` joins, `==` compares, `s[0]` is the first character, `s.length()` counts them.
- `>>` reads one word; `std::getline(std::cin >> std::ws, s)` reads a whole line.
